categoryIntros.nouns: Nouns name people, things, places, and ideas. They never change form; particles such as が and を mark their role in a sentence.
categoryIntros.pronouns: Pronouns stand in for a noun, such as これ (this), それ (that), and 自分 (oneself). Japanese often leaves them out when the context is clear.
categoryIntros.suru-verbs: Nouns that become verbs with する, as 紹介 (introduction) becomes 紹介する (to introduce), and する itself.
categoryIntros.godan-verbs: Godan verbs change their last kana across the five vowel sounds as they conjugate, as 言う becomes 言わない and 言います.
categoryIntros.ichidan-verbs: Ichidan verbs end in る after an i or e sound and drop the る to conjugate, as 見る becomes 見ない and 見ます.
categoryIntros.irregular-verbs: Verbs that follow neither the godan nor the ichidan pattern: 来る (to come) and the verbs ending in ずる, such as 信ずる (to believe). する and its compounds are under suru verbs.
categoryIntros.transitive-verbs: Transitive verbs take a direct object, usually marked with を, as 使う (to use) does in 道具を使う (to use a tool).
categoryIntros.intransitive-verbs: Intransitive verbs take no direct object, such as 有る (to be) and 行く (to go). Many pair with a transitive verb, as 出る (to leave) does with 出す (to take out).
categoryIntros.auxiliary-verbs: Auxiliary verbs follow another verb to add tense, politeness, or the passive, as た, ます, and れる do.
categoryIntros.i-adjectives: I-adjectives end in い and conjugate on their own, as 高い (high) becomes 高くない and 高かった.
categoryIntros.na-adjectives: Na-adjectives take な before a noun, as in 必要な物 (something necessary), and conjugate with だ and です.
categoryIntros.no-adjectives: Nouns that describe another noun with の, as 本当 does in 本当の話 (a true story).
categoryIntros.taru-adjectives: Literary adjectives that take たる before a noun, or と as an adverb, as 堂々 does in 堂々と (with dignity).
categoryIntros.pre-noun-adjectives: Pre-noun adjectives (rentaishi) come only before a noun and never conjugate, as この (this), そんな (such), and 大きな (big) do.
categoryIntros.adverbs: Adverbs say how, when, or how much, such as もう (already), ちょっと (a little), and こう (like this).
categoryIntros.expressions: Phrases of more than one word that JMdict lists as one entry, such as 宜しく (please treat me well) and 世の中 (the world).
categoryIntros.interjections: Words that stand on their own as exclamations or replies, such as はい (yes), ああ (ah), and 有難う (thank you).
categoryIntros.conjunctions: Conjunctions join words, clauses, or sentences, such as そして (and then), けれど (but), and ながら (while).
categoryIntros.particles: Particles follow a word to mark its role in a sentence or add nuance, such as は (the topic), を (the object), and ね (seeking agreement).
categoryIntros.counters: Counters follow a number to count a kind of thing, such as 枚 for flat things, 個 for small things, and 回 for times.
categoryIntros.prefixes: Prefixes attach to the front of a word, such as 不 (un-), 超 (super-), and 第, which makes ordinal numbers.
categoryIntros.suffixes: Suffixes attach to the end of a word, such as 的 (-ical), くらい (about), and みたい (-like).
categoryIntros.numbers: Numerals, such as 十 (ten), 百 (hundred), 千 (thousand), 万 (ten thousand), and 億 (hundred million).
categoryIntros.onomatopoeia: Giongo imitate sounds, such as どんどん (banging), and gitaigo describe states and movements, such as ゆっくり (slowly) and しっかり (firmly).
categoryIntros.yojijukugo: Yojijukugo are idioms of four kanji, many from Chinese classics, such as 不可思議 (a mystery) and 有耶無耶 (vague).
categoryIntros.proverbs: Kotowaza are traditional sayings that give advice or state a truth, such as 愛は盲目 (love is blind).
categoryIntros.idioms: Expressions whose meaning isn’t the sum of their words, such as 奥の手 (an ace up one’s sleeve) and 瓜二つ (exactly alike).
categoryIntros.honorific-language: Sonkeigo raises the person spoken about, as いらっしゃる does for 行く and 来る, and なさる does for する.
categoryIntros.humble-language: Kenjōgo lowers the speaker and their side to show respect to others, as 参る does for 行く and 頂く does for もらう.
categoryIntros.polite-language: Teineigo is the everyday polite register, built on です and ます, with words such as ござる.
categoryIntros.slang: Informal words and senses used among friends or within groups, such as キモイ (gross).
categoryIntros.internet-slang: Words and senses used mostly online, on message boards and social media, such as ツイ (Twitter) and イッチ (the original poster).
categoryIntros.manga-slang: Words used mostly in or about manga and anime, such as 萌えキャラ (a cute character).
categoryIntros.colloquialisms: Casual spoken words and forms, such as じゃん (isn’t it?) and 色んな (various).
categoryIntros.familiar-language: Words used with friends, family, or people below the speaker, such as お前 (you) and こいつ (this guy).
categoryIntros.formal-language: Formal and literary words, used in writing and speeches rather than conversation, such as 昨年 (last year) and べし (should).
categoryIntros.poetic-words: Words used in poetry and lyrical writing, such as 今宵 (this evening) and 暁 (dawn).
categoryIntros.childrens-language: Words young children use, or that adults use with them, such as 抱っこ (being carried in someone’s arms) and ぽんぽん (tummy).
categoryIntros.feminine-language: Words and sentence endings used mostly by women, such as かしら (I wonder) and あら (oh!).
categoryIntros.masculine-language: Words and sentence endings used mostly by men, such as 俺 (I), お前 (you), and ぜ.
categoryIntros.jocular-words: Words used humorously or tongue in cheek, such as 社畜 (a corporate drone).
categoryIntros.euphemisms: Gentler words for death, the body, and other delicate subjects, such as 亡くなる (to pass away).
categoryIntros.abbreviations: Shortened words and phrases, such as スマホ (smartphone, from スマートフォン) and 高校 (high school, from 高等学校).
categoryIntros.archaic-words: Words and senses from older Japanese that are no longer in everyday use, such as ござる (to be).
categoryIntros.obsolete-words: Words and senses that have fallen out of use, such as 文房 (a study).
categoryIntros.dated-words: Words that sound old-fashioned today but are still understood, such as 婦人 (lady) and 吾輩 (I).
categoryIntros.historical-terms: Words for things of the past, such as 明治 (the Meiji era), 侍 (samurai), and ソ連 (the Soviet Union).
categoryIntros.kana-words: Words that have kanji but are usually written in kana, such as する (to do), 事 (thing), and 有る (to be).
categoryIntros.kansai-dialect: Words from the Kansai region around Osaka, Kyoto, and Kobe, such as ほんま (truth) and しんどい (tired).
categoryIntros.osaka-dialect: Words from Osaka, such as いちびり (a joker) and パチる (to steal).
categoryIntros.kyoto-dialect: Words from Kyoto, such as ぶぶ漬け (rice with tea poured over it).
categoryIntros.tohoku-dialect: Words from the Tōhoku region in the north of Honshu, such as べこ (cow) and めんこい (adorable).
categoryIntros.kanto-dialect: Words from the Kantō region around Tokyo, such as 落っこちる (to fall) and 落っことす (to drop).
categoryIntros.kyushu-dialect: Words from Kyūshū, such as ばってん (but) and 濃ゆい (deep, of a colour).
categoryIntros.hokkaido-dialect: Words from Hokkaidō, such as なまら (very) and ザンギ (deep-fried chicken).
categoryIntros.ryukyu-dialect: Words from the Ryūkyū Islands and Okinawa, such as ゴーヤ (bitter melon) and チャンプルー (an Okinawan stir-fry).
categoryIntros.tosa-dialect: Words from Tosa, today’s Kōchi Prefecture on Shikoku, such as いごっそう (a stubborn person).
categoryIntros.tsugaru-dialect: Words from Tsugaru, in the west of Aomori Prefecture, such as わや (very).

privacy.intro: This policy covers the {name} iPhone app, Tomodachi for iPhone and Mac, zenbujapanese.com, and your Zenbu account.

short.heading: The short version
short.works: The app works without an account, and keeps what you do in it on your device.
short.reports: When the app crashes or freezes, it sends us a report without anything you read, type, say, or photograph, unless you turn crash reports off. If you report a problem, we get what you write.
short.account: If you create a Zenbu account, we keep your email, how you sign in, and the study data you sync, so your devices stay in step. If you subscribe, we keep a record of your subscription and payments; Apple or Stripe takes the payment itself.
short.noSale: We don't sell or share your personal information, and the app has no ads, usage analytics, or tracking.
short.providers: A few companies help us run the service, such as Cloudflare, which carries our traffic, and useSend, which sends our email.
short.rights: You can see, export, correct, or delete your data, and delete your account any time.

device.heading: On your device
device.storage: You never need an account. The app keeps your profile, searches, notes, known words, lists, watch history, photos, and Translate conversations in its private storage on your device, and sends us none of it unless you sign in to a Zenbu account, which syncs only what's listed below. It stays until you delete it in the app or uninstall the app, which doesn't delete a Zenbu account. Your device's own backups, such as iCloud Backup, can include it, under Apple's terms.
device.onDevice: Image Search, Translate, text recognition, and speech run on your device with Apple's frameworks. Translate uses the microphone only while a conversation or Listening is running, and hears whoever is speaking nearby, but keeps no audio and never sends a conversation to us. The app asks for the camera and microphone only when a feature needs them, and you can change that in iPhone Settings.
device.youtube: Player plays and searches YouTube videos, and can show YouTube's caption translations, so YouTube (Google) receives those requests under its own privacy policy. Optional dictionaries you download are delivered by Cloudflare.

reports.heading: Crash and problem reports
reports.crashes: When the app crashes, freezes, or is closed by iOS while you're using it, it sends a crash report to Sentry, which collects them for us, so we can find and fix the cause. When a step such as syncing your account, installing an optional dictionary, or starting Translate fails, it sends a code for the step and how it failed, never the error's own message. Crash reports are on by default, and you can turn them off at any time with {sendCrashReports} in the app's Settings.
reports.includes: A crash report includes where in the app's code the problem happened, the app's version and build, the iOS version, your device's model and its state at the time (such as the memory in use), and a random identifier the app creates on your device, so we can tell how many devices a problem affects. A crash report doesn't link that identifier to your Zenbu account.
reports.never: A crash report never includes what you read, type, say, or photograph in the app, such as your searches, notes, lists, photos, or Translate conversations. Nor does it include your location, your device's name, or its language, region, and time zone. Before a report leaves your device, the app removes the file paths and names, links, email addresses, and quoted text it finds in error messages.
reports.problems: You can also tell us about a problem with {reportAProblem} in the app's Settings. A problem report holds what you write, the email address in the form for a reply, if there is one, and the details the form lists under {included}: the app's version and build, the iOS version, your device's model, whether you're signed in, whether crash reports are on, which optional dictionaries you've installed, and whether the microphone and camera are allowed. If you're signed in, the form fills in your Zenbu account's email, which you can change or clear; if you're signed out, it sends an email only if you add one. Sentry adds the same technical details and random identifier as a crash report, so we can see a report's email alongside the other reports from the same copy of the app, and your account's email links those reports to your Zenbu account. A problem report is sent even when crash reports are off, because you chose to send it.
reports.written: The app removes file paths, links, and email addresses from what you write, and sends the rest as you wrote it, so it can hold anything you type, such as a word you looked up. Leave out anything you'd rather not share. The app attaches nothing else: no screenshots, photos, searches, lists, or conversations.
reports.ipAddress: Sentry receives your IP address with each report, as with any request over the internet, but we've set it not to store the address or the location it suggests.

account.heading: Your Zenbu account
account.intro: While you're signed out, our apps send nothing to our account service. If you create or sign in to a Zenbu account where our apps or this website offer one, we keep:
account.removals: Besides your study data, the iPhone app syncs its profile's name, username, and photo. When you remove something, such as a video, a list, a note, a photo, or a search, we keep only a record that it was removed, so your other devices follow, and a removed search keeps only a code that can't be turned back into it. We keep your photos' files in Cloudflare R2, apart from the account database and its backups. The profile's email and whole Translate conversations don't sync: a sentence you bookmark may be something someone else said, so only the sentences you bookmark leave your device. Deleting your account deletes everything it synced, your photos' files included. We'll update this policy before an app or this website syncs anything else.
account.emails: Our account service emails you only to send sign-in codes, to tell you when a way to sign in is added or removed, and to confirm that your account was deleted.
account.website: Where this website offers sign-in, your account there lets you change your name and username, manage how you sign in, subscribe and manage a subscription you bought here, sign out, and delete your account. It doesn't read your study data yet, and we'll update this policy before it does. Signing in uses cookies only to sign you in and keep you signed in, and the website remembers your theme and that you're signed in.

hiragana-to-katakana.first: Each hiragana has one katakana partner: <ja>か</ja> becomes <ja>カ</ja>, <ja>しゃ</ja> becomes <ja>シャ</ja>, and small kana stay small. The long-vowel mark <ja>ー</ja> belongs to both, so it carries over.
hiragana-to-katakana.second: Katakana mostly writes words from other languages, like <ja>コーヒー</ja> (coffee) and <ja>スマートフォン</ja> (smartphone), and names from outside Japan.

katakana-to-hiragana.first: Each katakana has one hiragana partner: <ja>カ</ja> becomes <ja>か</ja>, <ja>シャ</ja> becomes <ja>しゃ</ja>, and small kana stay small. The long-vowel mark <ja>ー</ja> belongs to both, so it carries over. <ja>ヷ</ja> to <ja>ヺ</ja> have no hiragana, so they stay as they are.
katakana-to-hiragana.second: Hiragana is how a learner reads a word aloud, so turning <ja>コーヒー</ja> into <ja>こーひー</ja> shows its sounds in the script you learned first.

romaji-to-kana.first: Type Japanese sounds in Latin letters and each syllable turns into kana as soon as it’s complete: <typed>ka</typed> becomes <ja>か</ja>, <typed>kya</typed> becomes <ja>きゃ</ja>. Letters that can’t start a syllable yet wait for the next one.
romaji-to-kana.second: Choose hiragana for Japanese words and katakana for words from other languages. A hyphen types the long mark, so <typed>ko-hi-</typed> becomes <ja>コーヒー</ja> in katakana.

kana-to-romaji.first: Each kana becomes its Hepburn spelling, the one on signs and in most textbooks: <ja>し</ja> is <latin>shi</latin>, <ja>つ</ja> is <latin>tsu</latin>, and <ja>ふ</ja> is <latin>fu</latin>. Katakana works the same way.
kana-to-romaji.second: Long vowels are spelled as they’re written: <ja>とうきょう</ja> is <latin>toukyou</latin>, and <ja>ー</ja> repeats the vowel before it, so <ja>コーヒー</ja> is <latin>koohii</latin>. Kana has no spaces between words, so neither does the romaji, and kanji stay as they are.

half-width-to-full-width.first: Half-width characters are narrow versions from early computers that showed one byte per character. Each becomes its standard full-width form: <ja>ｶ</ja> becomes <ja>カ</ja>, and <latin>A</latin> becomes <ja>Ａ</ja>.
half-width-to-full-width.second: A voiced half-width kana is two characters, the kana and a separate mark (<ja>ｶﾞ</ja>). They join into one (<ja>ガ</ja>).

full-width-to-half-width.first: Each full-width character becomes its narrow form: <ja>カ</ja> becomes <ja>ｶ</ja>, and <ja>Ａ</ja> becomes <latin>A</latin>. A voiced kana splits into two characters, <ja>ガ</ja> into <ja>ｶﾞ</ja>.
full-width-to-half-width.second: Hiragana and kanji have no half-width form, so they stay as they are.

kanjiAndLetters.question: Does it change kanji or letters?
kanjiAndLetters.answer: No. Only kana change. Kanji, Latin letters, numbers, and punctuation stay as they are, so you can paste a whole sentence.

longMark.question: What happens to the long mark ー?
longMark.answer: Hiragana and katakana share it, so it carries over unchanged. コーヒー becomes こーひー, which is how a learner would read it.

katakana.question: When is katakana used?
katakana.answer: Mostly for words borrowed from other languages, like コーヒー (coffee), for names from outside Japan, and for emphasis, as italics are in English.

n.question: How do I type ん?
n.answer: Type n before a consonant or at the end of a word, where nn works too. Before a vowel or y, type n’ so it isn’t read as な or にゃ: kin’en gives きんえん, while kinen gives きねん.

smallTsu.question: How do I type a small っ?
smallTsu.answer: Double the consonant after it: kitte gives きって, and matcha gives まっちゃ.

romanization.question: Which romanization does it use?
romanization.answer: Hepburn, the spelling on signs, maps, and most textbooks: し is shi, つ is tsu, and ふ is fu. It also accepts the other common spellings when you type, such as si, tu, and hu.

halfWidthKatakana.question: What is half-width katakana?
halfWidthKatakana.answer: A narrow form of katakana from early computers that could only show one byte per character. It still turns up on receipts, bank statements, and old systems.

forms.question: Why do forms ask for full-width?
forms.answer: Many Japanese forms check for full-width (全角) characters, especially in name and address fields, and reject half-width ones.

hiragana.question: Does it change hiragana?
hiragana.answer: No. Hiragana has no half-width form, so it stays as it is either way.
